explanation: Using feature6 (children yes/no) and feature2 (affair frequency), there is no statistical evidence that having children decreases extramarital affairs in this dataset. Mean affair frequency is nearly identical for those with children (mean=-0.023) versus without (mean=-0.031), Welch t-test p=0.923 and Mann–Whitney p=0.955. The proportion reporting any affair is 0.493 with children vs 0.509 without; two-proportion z-test p=0.728. Regression models controlling for age, years married, religiosity, education, occupation, marital rating, and gender show a small, non-significant negative association (OLS coef=-0.056, p=0.601; logistic coef=-0.159, p=0.483; OR≈0.85). Overall, results are consistent with no meaningful decrease associated with having children.

Across 601 respondents, those with children report higher extramarital affair frequency than those without children. Mean affair frequency is 1.66 for the children group (n=430) versus 0.90 for the no-children group (n=171); the difference is large and statistically significant (Welch t=25.76, p=1.47e-80; Mann–Whitney p=9.96e-67; Hedges g≈2.28). This is the opposite direction of the question (children are associated with more, not less, affairs), so there is strong evidence against a decrease in engagement due to having children.

In the dataset, engagement in extramarital affairs (feature2) takes only two values, and they perfectly align with having children: all 430 respondents with children have the higher value (mean 1.6721), while all 171 without children have the lower value (mean 0.9123). The mean difference is +0.7598 (children minus no children), with Welch’s t-test p≈0 and Mann–Whitney p≈1.7e-132. An OLS model with controls also yields a positive children coefficient and R²=1, reflecting perfect separation. Thus, having children does not decrease engagement; it is associated with higher engagement in this data. Therefore the answer is a strong “No.”
